title: The Happiness Hypothesis: Finding Modern Truth in Ancient Wisdom
author: Jonathan Haidt
target_audience: General readers interested in the science of happiness
Readers curious about the intersection of modern science and ancient wisdom
core_themes: Ancient wisdom versus modern psychological science
The divided self and inner conflict
Role of adversity in personal growth
Virtue, meaning, and purpose in life
primary_purpose: To explore and analyze ten great ideas from ancient traditions, comparing them with evidence from contemporary psychological research to uncover what truly makes people happy and fulfilled.

structure_format.narrative_style: Conversational, analytical, synthesizing research and storytelling
structure_format.organization: Divided into ten chapters, each devoted to a key ancient idea or hypothesis about happiness

key_concepts_lessons: Our minds are often divided against themselves, like a rider and an elephant.
Ancient wisdom often contains psychological truths validated by modern research.
External circumstances matter, but internal perspective and relationships are crucial for happiness.
Adversity, when processed well, can foster growth and deeper happiness.
Happiness arises from discovering meaning, serving others, and engaging with intrinsic values.
Virtue and character, as advocated by ancient traditions, contribute deeply to personal and societal well-being.
style_tone: Balanced between scientific rigor and practical wisdom
notable_features: Bridges ancient philosophical insights with contemporary psychology
Integrates Eastern, Western, and modern viewpoints
Presents a balanced, nuanced view on the pursuit of happiness
Accessible summaries of psychological research for lay readers
cultural_historical_context: Written at a time of renewed public interest in happiness and positive psychology, the book draws on wisdom traditions from around the world and places them in conversation with late 20th and early 21st-century psychological research.
reception_impact: Widely praised for its clarity and thoughtfulness
Popular in academic and popular science circles
Credited with making psychological science engaging for the general public
Used in university courses on happiness, psychology, and philosophy
comparable_titles: Stumbling on Happiness by Daniel Gilbert
The Art of Happiness by the Dalai Lama and Howard Cutler
Man's Search for Meaning by Viktor Frankl
How Will You Measure Your Life? by Clayton Christensen
